massachusetts.enforce_note: Non-competes are allowed only if they meet the strict requirements of the Massachusetts Noncompetition Agreement Act, including a 12-month limit and garden-leave pay.
massachusetts.state_note: The employer must give the agreement by the earlier of the job offer or 10 business days before work starts, and must pay garden leave of at least half the worker's highest base salary during the restricted period or other agreed consideration.
massachusetts.threshold_note: There is no dollar earnings threshold, but non-competes are void against nonexempt (overtime-eligible) employees, students, minors, and workers fired without cause or laid off.

michigan.enforce_note: Non-competes are generally enforceable in Michigan if they are reasonable as to duration, geographic area, and type of work, and protect a legitimate competitive business interest.
michigan.state_note: A court can 'blue-pencil' (trim) an overbroad clause instead of throwing it out, and merely keeping the job can count as consideration for signing a non-compete.
michigan.threshold_note: Michigan has no earnings threshold; any employee can be bound if the restriction is reasonable.

minnesota.enforce_note: Almost all employee and independent-contractor non-competes signed on or after July 1, 2023 are void and unenforceable, with narrow exceptions for the sale or dissolution of a business.
minnesota.state_note: The ban applies only to agreements signed on or after July 1, 2023, and an employee who has to enforce it can ask the court for attorney fees.
minnesota.statute_name: Covenants Not to Compete Void in Employment Agreements
minnesota.threshold_note: There is no earnings threshold because the ban covers employees and independent contractors at every pay level, including executives.

mississippi.enforce_note: Non-competes are enforceable under judge-made common law if they are reasonable in duration, geographic scope, and activities restricted and protect a legitimate business interest.
mississippi.state_note: Non-competes are disfavored and the employer must prove the restriction is reasonable, and a court may refuse to enforce one against a worker fired arbitrarily or in bad faith.
mississippi.threshold_note: Mississippi has no earnings threshold; courts judge each agreement on reasonableness.

missouri.enforce_note: Non-competes are enforceable under Missouri case law if they are reasonable and no more restrictive than necessary to protect the employer's legitimate interests, such as trade secrets or customer contacts.
missouri.state_note: Courts can 'blue-pencil' an overbroad clause, and a non-solicitation clause of one year or less is treated as reasonable by statute (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 431.202).
missouri.threshold_note: Missouri has no earnings threshold; courts judge each agreement on reasonableness.

montana.enforce_note: Montana law strongly disfavors non-competes, and a court enforces one only as a limited partial restraint that is reasonable in time and place, based on good consideration, and protects a legitimate business interest.
montana.state_note: An employer that fires a worker without misconduct usually has no legitimate interest to enforce a non-compete (Wrigg v. Junkermier, 2011 MT 290).
montana.statute_name: Contracts in Restraint of Trade (Montana Code Annotated)
montana.threshold_note: Montana has no earnings threshold; enforceability turns on reasonableness and whether the employer has a legitimate business interest.

nebraska.enforce_note: Non-competes are governed entirely by court decisions and are upheld only if they are reasonable, not injurious to the public, no greater than necessary to protect a legitimate interest, and not unduly harsh on the worker.
nebraska.state_note: Nebraska courts allow only a narrow non-solicitation limit tied to customers the worker actually dealt with, and they will not rewrite ('blue-pencil') an overbroad clause, so the whole clause fails.
nebraska.threshold_note: Nebraska has no earnings threshold; courts apply a strict three-part reasonableness test.

nevada.enforce_note: Non-competes are void unless supported by valuable consideration, no broader than needed to protect the employer, not an undue hardship, and proportionate to the consideration, and they cannot apply to hourly-paid workers.
nevada.state_note: A court can trim an unreasonable clause instead of voiding it, and a worker who wins a challenge to a banned clause can recover attorney fees and costs.
nevada.threshold_note: A non-compete cannot apply to an employee paid solely on an hourly wage basis, not counting tips or gratuities, under a 2021 amendment.
nevada.wage_threshold: hourly-paid employees (paid solely on an hourly basis)

new hampshire.enforce_note: Non-competes are void for low-wage workers, and for everyone else they are enforceable only if reasonable under a three-part court test.
new hampshire.state_note: An employer that requires a non-compete must give the worker a copy before the worker accepts the job offer, or the agreement is unenforceable (RSA 275:70).
new hampshire.statute_name: Noncompete Agreements for Low-Wage Employees Prohibited
new hampshire.threshold_note: Non-competes are void for 'low-wage employees' earning 200% of the federal minimum wage or less ($14.50 an hour at the $7.25 federal minimum wage), so the line moves if the federal minimum wage changes.

new jersey.enforce_note: New Jersey has no non-compete statute, and courts enforce non-competes under a three-part reasonableness test from Solari and Whitmyer: the clause must protect a legitimate interest, impose no undue hardship, and not harm the public.
new jersey.state_note: Courts can 'blue-pencil' an overbroad clause, and bills to restrict non-competes (such as A5708/S4385) were pending in 2026 but had not been enacted.
new jersey.threshold_note: New Jersey has no earnings threshold; courts judge each agreement under the three-part reasonableness test.
